pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 63. Bowls sold: 90. Lane: kept (for now). Ama's mood: (she told me to write "proud"; I wrote it myself).*

The morning after the Lantern Festival, the lane looked like a giant had sneezed. Red paper scraps clung to the wet pavement. The lanterns drooped, their strings limp and heavy with rain. A stray dog sniffed a discarded balloon and yawned, showing teeth that looked like tiny white buttons. The air smelled of burnt sugar and cold smoke, a sticky, sweet haze that clung to the nose.

We were all standing in the middle of the aisle, still wearing our aprons. Uncle Feng was scratching his back. Auntie Ping was peeling a piece of tape off her glittery nail. I stood between them, watching the market association’s office at the far end.

At noon, a letter arrived. It was thick, cream-colored, and smelled of office ink. The chairman read it once, then twice. He did not say a word. He just held it up.

The crowd leaned in. Uncle Feng’s elbow accidentally bumped my shoulder. I didn’t move. I was waiting. The silence was loud, like the hum of the tea machine before it clicks on. I could hear my own heart beating in my ears, a steady, thumping drum against the quiet.
pages.image: A sleepy morning in a night market lane, wet pavement with red paper scraps, drooping lanterns, a small dog yawning, and a group of vendors in aprons crowded around a man holding a thick cream-colored letter, warm golden light filtering through mist.

pages.text:
"Kept," the chairman said. "For a year. On trial."

A cheer went up, though it was quiet and surprised. Then he read further. "The city invites the cooks to record their recipes for the heritage archive. In whatever way suits them."

Uncle Feng roared, a loud, booming sound that made the nearest lantern string shake. A single red lantern popped off its wire and tumbled to the ground with a soft thud, but he did not care. He was laughing, his round face bright red and his hands slapping together.

"Whatever way suits them," he repeated, nodding at me. "That means you can write it down, Lin. Or you can taste it until it’s right. Your call."

I looked at Ama. She was smiling, but her eyes were sharp. She tapped the ground with her plastic sandal. "Taste first," she said softly. "Talk later. But now, we can talk."

The lane felt lighter. The tension of the last sixty nights seemed to lift, like a heavy blanket finally taken off a bed. We were still here, and the pot was still hot.

pages.text:
Auntie Ping clapped her hands so hard her glittery nails clicked. "I am taking the Sky Mall booth on weekday afternoons," she announced, looking very serious. "And I keep the tea stall at night. Both. A person can have both."

Mr. Tsai, who had been silent, stepped forward holding a small, plain lantern. He hung it in the window of his empty spice shop, and the glass began to shine in the dark.

"Lin," he said, his voice slow and careful. "I am retiring. But I am not gone. We will roast the spices together in the back of Stall 19, every month. I will sit in the boss chair. I will supervise. It is a very good chair."

I felt a sudden, warm pressure in my chest, like holding a hot cup of tea for too long. Then I heard a voice from the back of the crowd. It was Jun’s father, standing near the shrimp pond and looking very shy.

"Uncle Feng," he said. "Is there room... at the end of the lane? For a fried-chicken cart?"

Uncle Feng stopped laughing and looked at Jun, then at his father, his face softening into a big, kind smile.

"I thought you would never ask," he said.

pages.text:
Later, the crowd thinned. Ama and I sat on our plastic stools, counting the takings. The coins clinked, a small, bright music. Ama’s wrist was bare now, and she turned it with ease.

"I am going to teach you Hokkien," she said. "One word a night. You will write it in the ledger."

I looked at the red notebook. It was full. Every page was dense with numbers and weather notes. "Ama," I said. "There is only one column left. And it’s for the bowls sold."

Ama looked at me, then at the notebook. She shrugged, a small, decisive movement. "Then make a new one."

I took my pencil. I used a ruler to draw a straight line down the right side of the page. It felt wrong, and right, all at once. I wrote at the top of the new column, in my best handwriting: *A word a night.*

Ama nodded. "Good," she said. "Now, the first word. *Chia̍h-pá-buē?*"

I wrote it down. The ink glistened for a second, then dried. It was a small mark, but it felt heavy with meaning. It was the beginning of a conversation that had lasted forty years, and would last for many more.

pages.text:
That evening, the lane was quiet. The lanterns were off, but the memory of their light remained. I sat at the stall table, the red notebook open before me. I wrote the final line of the season.

*Night 63. Bowls sold: 90. Lane: kept (for now).*

I paused. My pencil hovered over the line for *Ama’s mood*. I wrote: *proud.*

Then, in smaller letters, I added a line no one had ever seen before. *Lin’s mood: the same.*

I closed the notebook. The rubber band snapped shut with a soft click. I leaned back in my chair. My hair was still damp from the rain, and it smelled of star anise and ginger. I lifted my sleeve and sniffed it.

The scent was warm, deep, and familiar. It was not a smell to hide. It was not a mistake. It was home. I smiled, and I did not worry about the next night. I was ready for the next word.
